    Generating class imbalance¶

    Imbalance is a row-removing deficit: instead of (or in addition to) changing values, the generator drops rows — so Xt is smaller than X. Real datasets are rarely balanced: rare events, censored observations, or biased sampling processes skew the row distribution. This makes pipelines that assume balanced classes or uniform feature coverage fail in instructive ways.

    This notebook shows the two levers available in badgers:

    1. Acting on the observation process — resample rows directly, with the affected rows decided by a selector (RandomSamplingClassesGenerator, RandomSamplingTargetsGenerator, RandomSamplingFeaturesGenerator). These generators do not use a DGP.
    2. Acting on the data-generating process (DGP) — truncate the data to a quantile range of a fitted causal model's node (CausalImbalanceGenerator).

    Goal¶

    Remove rows so that some classes (or score regions) become under-represented — a row-removing deficit applied with selectors.

    Part A — Acting on the observation process (no DGP)¶

    Sample data from different classes¶

    What the selector does here: ClassSelector builds one boolean mask per class value from the given shares. The shares are fractions of the total row count, clipped to the rows available in each class; classes absent from the mapping are kept as-is. RandomSamplingClassesGenerator then drops exactly the affected rows.

    In [3]:
    Copied! 
    # WHO loses rows and how many: per-class share of the total row count
selector = ClassSelector("cls", column_mapping, {"cls": {0:0.1, 1:0.05, 2:0.15, 3:0.2}}, rng=rng)
gen = RandomSamplingClassesGenerator(random_generator=rng)
Xt, _ = gen.generate(X=X.copy(), selector=selector)
print('row-removing:', X.shape, '->', Xt.shape)

    Sample data proportionally to a column (weighted resampling)¶

    What the selector does here: ProportionalSelector("f0", ...) returns per-row float scores in [0, 1] — the deficit probability grows with the value of f0. The consumer, RandomSamplingTargetsGenerator, resamples rows with probability proportional to 1 - score: rows with a HIGH deficit probability are largely dropped, rows with a LOW deficit probability are kept (and can even be replicated). The result concentrates on small-f0 rows — a form of imbalance driven by a continuous column.

    For illustration we also compute a demo ranking variable score and use it as a color: it is not a target and plays no role in the selection.

    In [6]:
    Copied! 
    # demo ranking variable for coloring only (y is deprecated as a data carrier)
score = -2 * X[:, 0] + 3 * X[:, 1] + 5

# WHO loses rows: deficit probability proportional to f0
selector = ProportionalSelector("f0", {"f0": 0, "f1": 1, "cls": 2})
gen = RandomSamplingTargetsGenerator(random_generator=rng)
Xt, _ = gen.generate(X=X.copy(), selector=selector)
print('row-removing:', X.shape, '->', Xt.shape)

    Sample data based upon the features themselves¶

    RandomSamplingFeaturesGenerator takes a sampling_proba_func: a function from X (the whole feature matrix) to one sampling probability per row. Rows with a high probability are resampled more often into the output (the function defines the keep weights, the inverse view of the selector scores above). Below we make the sampling probability decrease linearly with f0, so the output concentrates on small-f0 rows again — this time expressed with a custom keep-probability function instead of a selector.

    In [8]:
    Copied! 
    def sampling_proba_func(X_):
    feature = X_[:, 0]
    return normalize_proba(
        (feature - np.min(feature)) / (np.max(feature) - np.min(feature))
    )

gen = RandomSamplingFeaturesGenerator(random_generator=rng)
Xt_feat, _ = gen.generate(X.copy(), sampling_proba_func=sampling_proba_func)
print('row-removing:', X.shape, '->', Xt_feat.shape)
    def sampling_proba_func(X_): feature = X_[:, 0] return normalize_proba( (feature - np.min(feature)) / (np.max(feature) - np.min(feature)) ) gen = RandomSamplingFeaturesGenerator(random_generator=rng) Xt_feat, _ = gen.generate(X.copy(), sampling_proba_func=sampling_proba_func) print('row-removing:', X.shape, '->', Xt_feat.shape)

    from badgers.generators.tabular_data.imbalance.causal import CausalImbalanceGenerator
import dowhy.gcm as gcm
from badgers.core.dgp.backends import GcmSCMDGP


def make_scm(graph):
    scm = gcm.StructuralCausalModel(graph)
    for node in graph.nodes:
        if not list(graph.predecessors(node)):
            scm.set_causal_mechanism(node, gcm.EmpiricalDistribution())
        else:
            scm.set_causal_mechanism(node, gcm.AdditiveNoiseModel(
                prediction_model=gcm.ml.create_linear_regressor()))
    return scm

    Part B — Acting on the data-generating process (DGP)¶

    CausalImbalanceGenerator truncates the dataset: it keeps only the rows whose perturbation node falls inside quantile_range. Since the kept rows are untouched (no structural equation is re-evaluated), the descendants are untouched too — the result is a pure subset: a dataset that is imbalanced — concentrated in one part of the perturbation node's range — while remaining structurally consistent by construction.

    CausalImbalanceGenerator accepts either the built-in quantile_range truncation rule, or an explicit selector — the same Selector objects as Part A decide which rows are dropped (row-removing polarity: an affected row is removed). With an explicit selector, perturbation_nodes/quantile_range are ignored.

    import networkx as nx
import pandas as pd

import dowhy.gcm as gcm
from badgers.core.dgp.backends import GcmSCMDGP

def generate_linear_data(graph, n_samples=100, rng=None, coefficients=None):
    """Generate data from a linear structural equation model."""
    nodes = list(nx.topological_sort(graph))
    if coefficients is None:
        coefficients = {}
        for node in nodes:
            parents = list(graph.predecessors(node))
            coefficients[node] = {p: rng.uniform(0.5, 2.0) * rng.choice([-1, 1]) for p in parents}
    column_mapping = {node: i for i, node in enumerate(nodes)}
    data = np.zeros((n_samples, len(nodes)))
    for node in nodes:
        i = column_mapping[node]
        parents = list(graph.predecessors(node))
        if not parents:
            data[:, i] = rng.normal(size=n_samples)
        else:
            for p, coef in coefficients[node].items():
                data[:, i] += coef * data[:, column_mapping[p]]
            data[:, i] += rng.normal(scale=0.1, size=n_samples)
    return data, column_mapping
    import networkx as nx import pandas as pd import dowhy.gcm as gcm from badgers.core.dgp.backends import GcmSCMDGP def generate_linear_data(graph, n_samples=100, rng=None, coefficients=None): """Generate data from a linear structural equation model.""" nodes = list(nx.topological_sort(graph)) if coefficients is None: coefficients = {} for node in nodes: parents = list(graph.predecessors(node)) coefficients[node] = {p: rng.uniform(0.5, 2.0) * rng.choice([-1, 1]) for p in parents} column_mapping = {node: i for i, node in enumerate(nodes)} data = np.zeros((n_samples, len(nodes))) for node in nodes: i = column_mapping[node] parents = list(graph.predecessors(node)) if not parents: data[:, i] = rng.normal(size=n_samples) else: for p, coef in coefficients[node].items(): data[:, i] += coef * data[:, column_mapping[p]] data[:, i] += rng.normal(scale=0.1, size=n_samples) return data, column_mapping

    Generate imbalance with an explicit selector¶
    The same selection machinery as Part A also plugs into the causal
generator: an affected row is dropped. Here a TopQuantileSelector
keeps rows where X is low (it affects the rows where X is high):
    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    In [21]:
    

    

    


    
Copied!


    
    

    

    from badgers.core.selectors import TopQuantileSelector

sel = TopQuantileSelector(
    variables="X", column_mapping=column_mapping, quantile=0.8,
)

Xt, yt = gen.generate(X.copy(), y=None, selector=sel)
print(f"output shape: {X.shape} -> {Xt.shape}")

Xt, yt = gen.generate(X.copy(), y=None, selector=sel)
print(f"output shape: {X.shape} -> {Xt.shape}")

quantile_range, or explicit selector

    
    

    

      

    • Imbalance is a row-removing deficit: Xt is smaller than X.
      • 

    • The selector (or sampling_proba_func) decides who is affected;
the generator realizes the decision.
      • 

    • Truncation keeps rows as-is — descendants are untouched, the subset
stays structurally consistent.
      • 

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    

    Takeaways¶
      

    • Imbalance is a row-removing deficit: the output has FEWER rows than the input.
      • 

    • Selectors quantify which rows are affected; intensities (rate, quantile) are constructor arguments.
      • 

    • CausalImbalanceGenerator needs no DGP: dropping rows never re-evaluates structural equations.
      •
